To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) wildfire professionals and residents in a wildland‐urban interface (WUI) community differ in their risk assessments for specific properties; (2) these differences are not well explained either by objective measures of risk or by residents' perceptions of the risks they face; and (3) the nature of these differences suggests that the risk assessments of residents are based on a different set of factors from those used by professionals, and that these differences in the factors used to make risk assessments can explain a significant

(1) risk perception gaps exist between wildfire professionals and the public, (2) the nature of those gaps differs from what is typically found in other risk contexts, and (3) the risk perceptions of the public are not well explained in the context of this study by factors commonly found to influence risk perceptions.

the risk assessments made by a wildfire professional and by residents of private properties in a wildland-urban interface community diverged for the vast majority of properties and that these divergences were not well explained by commonly studied factors that are thought to affect risk perceptions.

the risk perception gap between wildfire professionals and residents in the WUI.
the nature of risk perception gaps and how these gaps relate to the specific level of individual risk faced by residents.
the nature of risk perception gaps and their potential implications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk perception gap exists and is not well understood.
risk perception is more complex than a single, overall measure of risk, and that it is not well represented by such a measure.
the risk perception gaps between residents and wildfire professionals are not well understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are many ways that risk perception can be measured and many different ways that risk perception and risk assessment can be compared.
there is no simple explanation for the observed differences between the risk perceptions of the professionals and the residents.
the risk assessments of wildfire professionals and the public diverge, and that the nature and causes of this divergence are complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, even when the public and experts agree on the overall level of risk, there can be substantial gaps between their assessments of the specific level of risks faced by individuals.
the risk perception gap between professionals and the public may not be a simple function of differences in risk information.
risk perception gaps are not limited to overall risk judgments, and they are not well explained simply by demographic or attitudinal factors.
